title: The Lack of Selfless Leadership
author: Aaron Renn
summary: In a shortened weekly digest, Aaron Renn builds on comments by Andrew Manshel, the longtime number two at New York's Bryant Park, that big-city public space suffers from a lack of selfless civic leadership. Manshel's point is that today's wealthy board members got ahead by advancing their own interests and carry that habit into non-profit service, unlike the generation that led the Bryant Park restoration. Renn says this confirms a theme of his own work, the decline of leadership at both the national and local level. He adds two observations of his own: that naming rights now go to anyone with money, in contrast to Indiana University's Herman B. Wells Rule, and that civic boards fill with strivers who treat every activity as a resume item. The digest also excerpts the writer Drunk Wisconsin on why people should hold on to their college friends.
points: Manshel argues that civic dysfunction stems from wealthy board members who are used to getting their way, want their names on things, and seek short-term results.
The Bryant Park restoration was led by people motivated by repairing the public sphere after New York's 1970s financial collapse, and that generation has not been replaced.
Renn notes that the old Herman B. Wells Rule, which barred naming a building for a person until five years after death, has given way to naming rights for sale.
Strivers who see all of life as resume building bring a risk-averse, self-advancing mindset into non-profit board service, often without realizing it.
The digest closes with a case for staying close to college friends as a defense against adult loneliness.
quotes: Today’s wealthy individuals got that way because they were aggressive at advancing their personal interests and they are used to getting their way. They bring this perspective to their service on non-profit boards.
Today’s civic leaders want their name on things and are looking for short term results. They are impatient and highly opinionated.

There was also a certain desperation among major property owners about the wiping out of the value of their investments as a result of perceived urban decay. Those owners were willing to try anything to preserve their capital and to take big swings.
One of the themes of my work has been the decline of leadership in the last few decades, at both the national and local level.

When I was a student at Indiana University, the school held to something called the “Herman B. Wells Rule,” named after a former university president. No building could be named after a person until at least five years after that person’s death.

our society forms strivers to view everything about their life as a résumé building activity for further upwards personal advancement. So high school students start a non-profit to burnish their college application, for example.

Those people likely often bring the same mindset to their service on non-profit boards as adults, even if they aren’t conscious of it. At a minimum, they have to be very risk averse in their service there to avoid adverse professional consequences.
